notes.text: Thou shall die — That is, thou shalt lose all the happiness thou hast either in possession or prospect; and thou shalt become liable to death, and all the miseries that preface and attend it. This was threatened as the immediate consequence of sin. In the day thou eatest, thou shalt die - Not only thou shalt become mortal, but spiritual death and the forerunners of temporal death shall immediately seize thee. See note at "ver. 17" 18, 19, 20. It is not good that man - This man, should be alone - Though there was an upper world of angels, and a lower world of brutes, yet there being none of the same rank of beings with himself, he might be truly said to be alone. And every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air God brought to Adam-Either by the ministry of angels, or by a special instinct that he might name them, and so might give a proof of his knowledge, the names he gave them being expressive of their inmost natures. See note at "ver. 18"

glossa.text:
« The Lord God therefore took, » etc. ((AUG., ubi supra, c. 8.)) He has already said that man was placed in paradise. Now he recapitulates to what end he was placed there, « that he might dress it, » etc. For it is not credible that God condemned him to labour before sin, etc., *as far as* whence Eccli. X: « for the beginning of man's pride is to fall away from God. »

« The Lord God therefore took the man, » etc. ((GREG., lib. XIX Moral., cap. 17, tom. I.)) It must be weighed that good things cannot profit, if the evils that creep in are not guarded against, etc., *as far as* but by growing proud under them they sink beneath them.

« And the Lord God took, » etc. ((HIERON. Quaest. Hebr. in Gen., tom. III.)) For « pleasure » the Hebrew has « Eden. » The Seventy themselves, therefore, have rendered it now « Eden, » now « pleasure. » But Symmachus, who « had before translated it a flowering paradise, here put « pleasantness, » or « delights. »

« And he put him, » etc. ((ISID.)) *Mystically.* From that which is added, « And that he should keep it, it is hinted what kind of work it was: because in the tranquillity of the blessed life, where death is not, all work is to keep what thou holdest. For a precept was given, that they should take of every tree of paradise, but not of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil: that is, that they should not so enjoy it as to violate the integrity of their nature by usurping what was forbidden.

« And he enjoineth him, » etc. ((AUG., ubi supra, c. 13.)) He was forbidden from the tree, etc., *as far as* what lies between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience.

((AUG., ubi supra, c. 17.)) It is asked whether to the man alone, or to the woman also, etc., *as far as* « let them ask their husbands at home. »

((PROCOP. in Gen. )) Some say: If he willed to clothe us with immortality, what need was there of a precept, on account of which we were to sin and then to feel the severe stings of his judgment? I answer: Since he is kind and gentle, and willed to lay claim to the human race for an incorruptible and immortal condition: lest they should set that benefit down to their own or proper power, he acted in this manner, he willed that they should render him thanks, and for them he also appointed the present life as a wrestling-school and, as it were, a schooling for the life to come. Then, bringing in death on account of sin, he willed that we should acknowledge our infirmity, and that thereafter we ourselves should the more desire the gift to come.

« And he commanded him, saying: Of every, etc. ((AUG. de Gen. ad litt., l. VIII, 28, tom. III.)) If it be asked how he spoke these things, it cannot properly be comprehended by us. For it is certain that he speaks either through his own substance, etc., *as far as* but through a creature subject to himself.

It is asked: how could they speak, or understand one speaking, who had not learned by growing up among speakers, or by teaching? But God had made them such as could speak, and could learn from others if there were any.

((AUG., ubi supra, c. 14.)) Of Christ it is said, Isa. VII: « Before the child knows good or evil, he shall despise wickedness, that he may choose the good. » How does he either despise or choose what he does not know? etc., *as far as* what he ought not to have lost.

« But of the tree, » etc. ((AUG., ubi supra, c. 15.)) The tree from this, etc., *as far as* that is, that they were not about to lose what they loved.

((SEVERIANUS.)) There were three differences of trees in paradise. One indeed had been given him that he might live, another that he might live well, the third that he might live always.


« For in whatsoever day, » etc. He does not say, If thou eat, thou shalt be mortal, but « thou shalt die the death. » For man died in his soul when he sinned, because God withdrew from him, who is the life of the soul: upon which followed the death of the body, the soul departing from him, which is the life of the body; and this befell Adam when he ended the present life. It can be understood thus, that when they sinned, they were at once punished with that death of which it is said in Rom. seven: « Unhappy man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? » and in the same, chapter eight: « The body is dead because of sin; » he does not say mortal, but « dead, » although it is mortal, because it is to die. It is not to be believed that before sin those bodies were so, [0089B] but animal, not yet spiritual, yet not dead — bodies, that is, which must needs die, which came about on the day of the transgression.

« Thou shalt die the death. » A twofold death is signified: that of the soul, the Lord departing, who is its life; or that of the body, which he received at the end of his life. But at once he incurred the necessity of dying.

notes.text: Imputeth — Whom God doth not charge with the guilt of his sins, but graciously pardons and accepts him in Christ. No guile - Who freely confesses all his sins, and turns from sin to God with all his heart.

Silence — From a full and open confession of my sins. Old - My spirit failed, and the strength of my body decayed. Roaring - Because of the continual horrors of my conscience, and sense of God's wrath.
Hand — Thy afflicting hand. My moisture - Was dried up.
The iniquity — The guilt of my sin.

For this — Upon the encouragement of my example. Found - In an acceptable and seasonable time, while God continues to offer grace and mercy. Waters - In the time of great calamities. Not come - So as to overwhelm him.
I will — This and the next verse seems to be the words of God, whom David brings in as returning this answer to his prayers. Mine eye - So Christ did St. Peter, when he turned and looked upon him.
Will not — Unless they be forced to it by a bit or bridle. And so all the ancient translators understand it.

Sorrows — This is an argument to enforce the foregoing admonition. The Psalmist exhorts the righteous to praise God, for his truth, justice and goodness, ver. 1-5, For creating the world, ver. 6-9. For his providence in governing it, ver. 10-17. For his peculiar favour to his people, encouraging them to trust in him, ver. 18-22.

glossa.text: *Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven,* etc. ((AUG.)) Not those in whom he finds no sin, but those to whom he forgives it. *Iniquities.* He means the tinder of sin, namely concupiscence, etc., *as far as* but that sin may be no more. ((HIERON.)) Iniquities, before faith and baptism: sin, after faith and baptism.

*Blessed is the man.* ((HIERON.)) To whom God forgives, for not of himself. He covers it, that it be not revealed in the judgment; and so it will not be imputed unto punishment. There is no guile in him that accuses himself: he holds in the heart what he confesses here with the mouth.

*Blessed:* because formerly, not confessing to God, I came into sin, while I cried out, if I did any good.

*I was silent.* ((AUG.)) He who will not confess his sins labours without cause in the defence of sins: and since in this he also boasts of his merits, his strength fails the more. ((CASS.)) *Blessed is he to whom he hath not imputed.* To some, who have grievous sins, God imputes them; to others he does not impute them, through mercy, even though they have some — namely to those who do not proclaim themselves just when they are evil, but acknowledging themselves make satisfaction. This I now profess, but formerly: *Because I was silent,* etc. ((AUG.)) Or, *I was silent,* as to sin with my voice, *while I cried out all the day:* while the penalty of sin, or an inward blinding, showed me a sinner, or while my evil life cried out, though I was silent, whether I had done any good.

*While I cried out all the day,* etc. Although a man be not conscious to himself of anything, yet he is not just: for who understands his offences? Whence: *There is a just man that perisheth in his own justice.* And the Apostle: *I am conscious to myself of nothing,* etc.
*The thorn is fastened in.* ((CASS.)) *The thorn,* which lifts up the whole body, that is, pride. ((AUG.)) Likewise *misery,* etc., *as far as: in the hands of a drunken man.*
*My sin.* Diapsalma. Confession, whence pardon, as above the growing old from governance. *I have made known.* ((CASS.)) For *I said* before, etc., *as far as* and God hears.

*For this shall he pray.* ((ID.)) Diapsalma. Commending repentance, he says it is common to all the saints; which sundry sects reject, against whom he flees for refuge to God. ((AUG.)) *For this.* Therefore every saint prays, because thou hast forgiven, otherwise he would not be a saint. *In the time,* etc. It is the time of grace, the law, pressing and convicting the guilty, compelled them to cry out, grace heals. *But yet in the flood,* etc. ((AUG.)) Although the saint pray, etc., *as far as* the saint will pray, saying: *Thou art a refuge. To him.* That is, to God, for he changes the person, as often. They do not draw near who say that fate makes them sin, or fortune, which rules all things, or the people of darkness, which rebels against God.

*I will give thee understanding.* ((ID.)) Diapsalma. It is answered to the penitent: *I will give thee understanding,* etc. Behold a psalm of understanding, lest the suppliant be thought neglected, with God for witness. *Thou, deliver.* ((CASS.)) Thou who hast promised, *I will give thee understanding.* Or Christ answers the penitent: A glad end, God gives understanding: whence he exhorts others to the same.

*Become ye not as the horse and the mule,* etc. ((AUG.)) Having received understanding, this penitent turns himself to the proud who defend their sins: therefore you, whom I invite, etc. *The horse,* the untamed Gentile; *the mule,* the Jew slow to believe. ((CASS.)) *The horse,* without discernment of its riders; *the mule,* takes any burdens whatever, etc., *as far as* that is, boasting of one's own strength. *Their jaws.* Or, *the jaws* with which they chew, that is, give victuals more sparingly, that being compelled by necessity they may return. ((AUG.)) Or, thou wilt break them here, and in the world to come there will be many scourges. Or: *Become ye not as the horse,* because there are many scourges here and in the world to come. *Who come not near to thee.* ((CASS.)) For there are those who, if they sin through the weakness of the flesh, do not withdraw from devout prayers.

*Many are the scourges of the sinner,* etc. ((AUG.)) After the bridle, scourges are added for taming, lest he be of those unpunished ones to whom a roving licence of their own way is now given: so this man above said that he was tamed.

notes.text: Therefore — This refers to all the preceding discourse; from which the apostle infers what follows. He does not therefore properly make a digression, but returns to speak again of sin and of righteousness. As by one man - Adam; who is mentioned, and not Eve, as being the representative of mankind. Sin entered into the world - Actual sin, and its consequence, a sinful nature. And death - With all its attendants. It entered into the world when it entered into being; for till then it did not exist. By sin - Therefore it could not enter before sin. Even so - Namely, by one man. In that - So the word is used also, 2 Cor. v, 4. All sinned - In Adam. These words assign the reason why death came upon all men; infants themselves not excepted, in that all sinned.

For until the law sin was in the world — All, I say, had sinned, for sin was in the world long before the written law; but, I grant, sin is not so much imputed, nor so severely punished by God, where there is no express law to convince men of it. Yet that all had sinned, even then, appears in that all died.

Death reigned — And how vast is his kingdom! Scarce can we find any king who has as many subjects, as are the kings whom he hath conquered. Even over them that had not sinned after the likeness of Adam's transgression - Even over infants who had never sinned, as Adam did, in their own persons; and over others who had not, like him, sinned against an express law. Who is the figure of him that was to come - Each of them being a public person, and a federal head of mankind. The one, the fountain of sin and death to mankind by his offense; the other, of righteousness and life by his free gift. Thus far the apostle shows the agreement between the first and second Adam: afterward he shows the differences between them. The agreement may be summed up thus: As by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; so by one man righteousness entered into the world, and life by righteousness. As death passed upon all men, in that all had sinned; so life passed upon all men, (who are in the second Adam by faith,) in that all are justified. And as death through the sin of the first Adam reigned even over them who had not sinned after the likeness of Adam's transgression; so through the righteousness of Christ, even those who have not obeyed, after the likeness of his obedience, shall reign in life. We may add, As the sin of Adam, without the sins which we afterwards committed, brought us death; so the righteousness of Christ, without the good works which we afterwards perform, brings us life: although still every good, as well as evil, work, will receive its due reward.

Yet not — St. Paul now describes the difference between Adam and Christ; and that much more directly and expressly than the agreement between them. Now the fall and the free gift differ,

1. In amplitude, ver. 15.

2. He from whom sin came, and He from whom the free gift came, termed also "the gift of righteousness," differ in power, ver. 16.

3. The reason of both is subjoined, ver. 17.

4. This premised, the offense and the free gift are compared, with regard to their effect, ver. 18, and with regard to their cause, ver. 19.

The sentence was by one offense to Adam's condemnation — Occasioning the sentence of death to pass upon him, which, by consequence, overwhelmed his posterity. But the free gift is of many offenses unto justification - Unto the purchasing it for all men, notwithstanding many offenses.
There is a difference between grace and the gift. Grace is opposed to the offense; the gift, to death, being the gift of life.
Justification of life — Is that sentence of God, by which a sinner under sentence of death is adjudged to life.

As by the disobedience of one man many (that is, all men) were constituted sinners — Being then in the loins of their first parent, the common head and representative of them all. So by the obedience of one - By his obedience unto death; by his dying for us. Many - All that believe. Shall be constituted righteous - Justified, pardoned.

glossa.text:
*Therefore.* He said that justice and life are through Christ. And that it can be through him, he intends to prove by a likeness in the lesser case.

*Through one.* Namely Adam: the Apostle did not say one Eve, holding to the custom, in that he attributes the succession of human posterity (which succumbs to the sin and the death coming from him) not to the woman, but to the man. For posterity is not wont to be named from the woman, but from the man. Or, because the woman is from the man, and of both there is one flesh. Whether therefore it be said from Eve or from Adam, either pertains to the first man: and by this the Apostle willed original sin to be understood as the sin of propagation, whose chief is Adam, not of imitation, whose chief is the devil; whence: *By the envy of the devil death entered into this world.* 

 *Unto all men.* Because even before the law, when it did not so seem, the law not teaching it, sin was indeed imputed among men, but not with God, as sinners supposed, with whom it was thought that it would go unpunished, since it was not known that he would judge: but when the law was given, they came to know that God cares for human things and judges them. Before, it was not imputed, but death reigned securely, the devil possessing men by reason of the impunity that was believed in, until Moses, through whom the knowledge of the one God returned. Death therefore reigned (as another reading has it), yet not unto all, but unto those like Adam the transgressor, who, God being neglected, served the creature, as he consented to the devil in the place of God. Such were almost all until the law. Very few, like Abraham, served the one God, and over them death did not reign; rather they were kept in hope, to be freed at the coming of Christ.

*Until the law,* etc. That is, because neither could the law take away sin, but increased it, whether the natural law or the written: but it was not imputed, that is, it was not known: yet it reigned until Moses, that is, until the law: because neither could the law itself take away the reign of death, which reigns while it does not allow the guilt of sin to come to eternal life, but drags it to Gehenna. This reign the grace of Christ alone destroyed, even among the ancients: apart from whom it reigned over all: even over those who did not sin by their own proper will, as Adam did, but were held by the original fault, as children are.

*But it reigned.* It was not imputed, but the effect showed it, because bodily death reigned daily through sundry sufferings, at last by dissolution, until Moses, when it was the less seen.

*Who is a figure.* Adam is the figure of Christ: because as he is the father of all according to the flesh, so is Christ according to faith; and as from the side of that one Eve was formed, so from the side of this one flowed forth the sacraments, by which the Church is saved. And therefore, as that one could impart to his sons sin and death, so this one imparts to his own his own justice and life; and this one moreover confers more of good upon his own than that one of evil: and therefore he is more able to save than that one to destroy.

*But not as,* etc. The figure lies in this, that one amends, one sinned; but the case of Adam is not such as the case of Christ: because one is the offence of Adam, by which many, that is, those transgressing in like manner, died; but the grace of Christ is unto more: because it is both unto these, and unto those not transgressing in like manner.

*For if. ((AMBR.))* Death reigned, it does not reign, because they who through the law, etc., *as far as* for there is not a general damnation or justification in all.

*Through one it reigned,* etc. Because what strength it had in him, it exercised upon all who came after, of whom he was the matter: just as the fault also, which was his alone, was poured over into all. *Much more,* etc. Because eternally, whereas death reigned in them temporally and with an end.

*Through the justice of one,* etc. Not that all begotten of Adam are regenerated through Christ, but as no man's carnal generation is except through Adam, so no man's spiritual generation is except through Christ. If there were any begotten apart from Adam, and any regenerated apart from Christ, he would not say *all* and *all.* But as there is no man apart from that generation, so there is no just man apart from this. The same men he afterwards calls *many.*

*For as,* etc. He determines the offence of one and the justice of one, so that, as that one destroyed by the desert of sin, so this one may be seen to have freed us by the desert of justice. *So also through the one,* etc. He says of the man, not the faith of God or of the Word, lest thou suppose that the just of old were freed in the Word of God alone, that is, by faith in the Word alone without faith in the incarnation.

notes.text: Then — After this glorious evidence of his Father's love, he was completely armed for the combat. Thus after the clearest light and the strongest consolation, let us expect the sharpest temptations. By the Spirit - Probably through a strong inward impulse. Mark i, 12; Luke iv, 1.

Having fasted — Whereby doubtless he received more abundant spiritual strength from God. Forty days and forty nights - As did Moses, the giver of the law, and Elijah, the great restorer of it. He was afterward hungry - And so prepared for the first temptation.
Coming to him — In a visible form; probably in a human shape, as one that desired to inquire further into the evidences of his being the Messiah.

It is written — Thus Christ answered, and thus we may answer all the suggestions of the devil. By every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God - That is, by whatever God commands to sustain him. Therefore it is not needful I should work a miracle to procure bread, without any intimation of my Father's will. Deut. viii, 3.

The holy city — So Jerusalem was commonly called, being the place God had peculiarly chosen for himself. On the battlement of the temple - Probably over the king's gallery, which was of such a prodigious height, that no one could look down from the top of it without making himself giddy.
In their hands — That is, with great care. Psalm xci, 11, 12.
Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God — By requiring farther evidence of what he hath already made sufficiently plain. Deut. vi, 16.
Showeth him all the kingdoms of the world — In a kind of visionary representation.
If thou wilt fall down and worship me — Here Satan clearly shows who he was. Accordingly Christ answering this suggestion, calls him by his own name, which he had not done before.
Get thee hence, Satan — Not, get thee behind me, that is, into thy proper place; as he said on a quite different occasion to Peter, speaking what was not expedient. Deut. vi, 13.
Angels came and waited upon him — Both to supply him with food, and to congratulate his victory.

glossa.text:
*Then Jesus.* After baptism, because there is no delay before temptation: that he may straightway teach the baptized to go out of the world, and in quiet to be free for God: so the sons of Israel after the passage of the sea go up through the desert, and eat manna until they come to the land of promise. *Then Jesus was led,* etc. ((RAB.)) This is the order of right converse, that after receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit we should gird ourselves the more closely against the devil: by that way the Samaritan came down, because clothed in flesh he bore the same temptations.

*To the Spirit*, the Holy, who sends strong to the battle those whom he fills. Without this Spirit, he who goes to the battle quickly falls. *That he might be tempted by the devil.* He is not tempted by the devil save because he has gone out to the desert, that is, has begun to be zealous for good.

*And when he had fasted. ((BEDA.))* He fasts that he may be tempted, he is tempted because he fasts, and he gives us an example of fasting, etc., *as far as* and so, as long as we are here, let us always bewail our sins: because by this number the present life is shown.

((LEO.)) While through the various actions of this life our solicitude is stretched out, it must needs be that from the dust of the world, etc., *as far as* that we, who have been raised together in his resurrection, may be found to have died together in his passion.

*Afterwards he was hungry.* This belongs to true humanity: and through this comes the occasion of tempting. The power lies hidden, the weakness lies open.

*And coming.* Because hunger is a sign of weakness. And so temptation is not wanting to us in abstinence. Through the outward weakness he tempts Christ, in whom he found no law of sin. *If thou be the Son of God.* It is one thing to be a man exploring these matters, another to be a man tempting, while he seems to confess God and endeavors to mock at one of this kind. For so he tempts, that he may explore what he fears. So he explores, that by tempting he may deceive. *If thou be the Son of God.* He had known that the Son of God had come into the world, whether by the prophets, or by the angels announcing it, or by John pointing him out: but because he saw humble things in him, what he had suspected concerning the Godhead came into doubt with him out of pride. Whence also he cunningly makes inquiry: Nor was it unworthy that Christ, who had come to be slain, should be tempted, that by overcoming temptations he might give us the power of overcoming temptations, as by his own death he took away our mortality.

((RAB.)) Christ did not suffer himself to be tempted except after baptism, hinting that those who come to him will suffer heavier things, etc., *as far as* but Christ was tempted by suggestion only: because the delight of sin did not bite his mind.

*It is written.* He does not use his power, but the authority of the Scriptures, teaching us to fight rather with doctrine than with miracles. *Not in bread alone doth man live.* As if to say: Thy persuasion is a temptation: because thou treatest of the food of the body, and not of the food of the mind. The lower part of man is sustained by bread, the other is refreshed by the word of God: but because thou treatest of the lower part, it is plain that thou art a tempter. *But in every word,* etc. Every word is charity, in which are fulfilled all the things that proceed out of the mouth of God, because by whosesoever ministry they are spoken, they are not his but God's: but if anything contrary is inserted, this is not of God. Out of the one word, that is, the wisdom of God, proceeds whatever the saints speak, who are his mouth.

*Then he took him.* The first and the last temptation were in the desert; the middle one, moreover, was historically the last, after he had returned to Jerusalem. Because Matthew follows not the order of the history, but the order of Adam's temptation: whereas Luke follows the order in which the thing was done.

Because he was left conquered and uncertain by Christ's answer: after the first he went on to the second temptation.

That he permitted himself to be taken up was not weakness, but patience: whereas in the devil it was not power, but pride.

Note that all these things were accomplished by the bodily senses. Nor is it a wonder if he permitted himself to be carried about: if the taking up is so understood, he who permitted himself to be crucified.

*Upon the pinnacle. ((RAB.))* In Palestine the roofs were flat on top, and there was the seat of the teachers, whence, etc., *as far as* he shows that we should obey whoever commands good and lofty things, but resist him who wills to cast us down.

*If thou be the Son. ((BEDA.))* In all the temptations he does this, that he may understand, etc., *as far as* it is likely that the devil appeared in the shape of a man.

*Cast thyself.* This voice befits him who busies himself to cast all men down: in which he is shown to be weak, because he can hurt no one, unless that man first cast himself down. For he was suggesting that by some sign he should explore how much he could avail with God. But no one ought to tempt God, when he has from human reason what he may do. Whence though he could do all things, he yet says to his own: *If they persecute you in this city, flee into another.* And he himself likewise fled and departed and hid himself. Now he could have come down from the temple otherwise than by casting himself down out of boastfulness. When human reason fails, let a man commend himself to God, not by tempting, but by devoutly confessing.

*For he hath given his angels charge over thee. ((BEDA.))* What is rightly said of the body, the devil wrongly interprets of the head, etc., *as far as* but he speaks of the help of the angels as though to a weak man, and is silent about his own being trodden underfoot.

*Again he took him.* This temptation went before in order, but is related out of its place, according to what was done in Adam's case.

*He showed him,* etc. Not that he enlarged the sight of him who sees all things, but the vanity of worldly pomp, which he loved, as though it were beautiful, etc., *as far as* Not that he beheld it with the eye of concupiscence as we do, but this showing was in the mind, as physicians see diseases without being harmed by them.

*All these will I give thee.* This he says out of arrogance: not that the whole world is his.

From the beginning the devil labored to usurp for himself what was God's: whence, that he might be worshipped in them, he invented idols. In these three are marked gluttony, avarice, pride.

((RAB.)) Luke sets avarice in the middle, and pride last, etc., *as far as* in these three all the kinds of temptations are comprehended.

*It is written.* David laid Goliath low with three stones from the torrent, and Christ laid the devil low with three testimonies from the law. *The Lord thy God.* This is either said to the devil: not because he was going to fulfil it out of devotion, but that, on the contrary to what he himself was attempting, it might be shown by what is written that not he, but God is to be adored: or he hints that this precept was given not to the devil, but to himself according to his humanity, and to any man whatsoever. Likewise also that other word: *Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God,* namely the Son and the Father and the Holy Spirit, who is one God. God is adored, and is served especially for his own sake.

Here it is shown that the man Christ, as God and Lord, is to be adored by debt.

*Thou shalt serve.* In Greek λατρεύσεις : for λατρεία is called service. Service common to God and to man and to whomsoever is called in Greek δουλεία. But that which is owed to God alone is called latria: whence idolatry, which gives to idols what it owes to God alone.

Note that the devil is conquered in those things in which he conquered Adam. Him he tempted by gluttony, when he asked him to taste of the forbidden tree. By vainglory, when he said ((Gen. III)): *You shall be as gods.* By avarice, when he said: *Knowing good and evil.*

*They came.* Not as though then coming to him for the first time, but beholding the Lord's contest from afar, lest he should seem to have needed their protection or to have conquered by it. But when the other went away conquered, they came ready for his service. As in this contest our warfare is laid out beforehand, so in the service of the angels a glorious recompense is taught.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely […]
echoes.note: "Sin entered into the world through one man" (5:12) figurally reads the Eden narrative: Adam's single transgression in eating the forbidden fruit is the entry point of sin into the cosmos. Paul explicitly types Adam as "a foreshadowing of him who was to come" (5:14, typos), making the fall the controlling figure for the Adam-Christ antithesis.

echoes.text: but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.”
echoes.note: "Death through sin... death passed to all" (5:12): "in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die." The divine sentence binding death to the one prohibited act is the textual basis for Paul's claim that death entered through the one man's transgression.

echoes.text: To Adam he said, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and ate from the tree, about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’ the ground is cursed for your sake. You will eat from it with much labor all the days of your life. It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field. By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, […]
echoes.note: "Death passed to all men" and "death reigned" (5:12, 5:14, 5:17): "cursed is the ground because of you... you are dust, and to dust you shall return." Adam's curse universalizing death is figurally taken up as the reign of death over all humanity that Christ's act of righteousness reverses.

echoes.text: When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate; and she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.
echoes.note: "Through the one man's disobedience many were made sinners" (5:19): "she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband, and he ate." Adam's specific act of disobedient eating is the trespass/parakoe Paul opposes to Christ's obedience (hypakoe).

echoes.text: Because God created man for incorruption, And made him an image of his own proper being; But by the envy of the devil death entered into the world, And those who are of his portion make trial thereof.
echoes.note: "Through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin" (5:12): "God created man for incorruption... but through the devil's envy death entered the world." The closest Second Temple parallel, sharing the precise idiom "death entered the world" (eiselthen... thanatos) and tracing universal death to a primeval cause. Paul localizes the cause in Adam's trespass rather than the devil's envy.

echoes.text: God said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?”
echoes.note: "Adam's disobedience" / "the one man's disobedience" (5:14, 5:19): "Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?" God's interrogation frames Adam's act precisely as disobedience to a command, supplying the parakoe Paul contrasts with Christ's obedience.

echoes.text: Adam lived one hundred thirty years, and became the father of a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth. The days of Adam after he became the father of Seth were eight hundred years, and he became the father of other sons and daughters. All the days that Adam lived were nine hundred thirty years, then he died. Seth lived one hundred five years, then became the father of Enosh. Seth lived after he became the father of Enosh eight […]
echoes.note: "Death reigned from Adam until Moses" (5:14): the tolling refrain "and he died" through the Sethite genealogy (Genesis 5) concretizes the unbroken reign of death over the generations between Adam and the giving of the law. Paul's historical span presupposes this litany of mortality.

echoes.text: From a woman was the beginning of sin; And because of her we all die.
echoes.note: "Through one... death" passed to all (5:12, 5:15): "From a woman sin had its beginning, and because of her we all die." A Second Temple text tracing universal death to the primeval transgression in Eden, structurally parallel to Paul (though Ben Sira blames Eve, Paul Adam). Strong thematic overlap on death-through-one.

echoes.text: God spoke all these words, saying, “I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. “You shall have no other gods before me. “You shall not make for yourselves an idol, nor any image of anything that is in the heavens above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth: you shall not bow yourself down to them, nor serve them, for I, Yahweh your God, am a jealous God, visiting the […]
echoes.note: "Death reigned from Adam until Moses" and "the law came in besides" (5:14, 5:20): the Sinai law-giving through Moses is the temporal boundary and the "law that came in" so that the trespass might increase. Paul presupposes the Mosaic legislation (Exodus 20 / the Decalogue) as the entry of nomos into his salvation-history scheme.

echoes.text: Out of the ground Yahweh God made every tree to grow that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food, including the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
echoes.note: "Grace... reign through righteousness to eternal life" (5:21): the tree of life in Eden (Genesis 2:9; 3:22-24), forfeited at the fall, faintly stands behind the restoration of "eternal life" through the second Adam. A disputed figural undertone rather than a verbal echo.

echoes.text: But they, like Adam, have broken the covenant. They were unfaithful to me, there.
echoes.note: "As through one trespass... all condemned" (5:18): "like Adam they transgressed the covenant" (one reading of Hosea 6:7) treats Adam as the archetypal covenant-breaker. A faint and textually disputed possible precedent for Paul's Adam-as-transgressor typology.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: He humbled you, and allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know; that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh’s mouth.
echoes.note: Jesus' first reply (v.4) quotes verbatim 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God.' High Volume (explicit 'It is written' + near-exact wording) and Thematic Coherence: Deut 8:3 interprets the wilderness manna as God's pedagogy to teach Israel dependence on his word; Jesus, fasting in the wilderness, recapitulates and passes the test Israel failed.

echoes.text: You shall not tempt Yahweh your God, as you tempted him in Massah.
echoes.note: Jesus' second reply (v.7) quotes 'You shall not test the LORD your God.' Formula 'it is written' + verbatim citation. In Deut 6:16 the warning is 'as you tested him at Massah' (water from the rock); Jesus refuses to coerce God's protective care, again reversing Israel's wilderness failure.

echoes.text: You shall fear Yahweh your God; and you shall serve him, and shall swear by his name.
echoes.note: Jesus' climactic reply (v.10) 'You shall worship the LORD your God, and you shall serve him only' quotes Deut 6:13 (LXX adds 'only/alone'). High Volume formula citation; the demand for exclusive worship answers Satan's demand to be worshiped (v.9).

echoes.text: For he will put his angels in charge of you, to guard you in all your ways. They will bear you up in their hands, so that you won’t dash your foot against a stone.
echoes.note: Satan's temptation (v.6) quotes verbatim 'He will command his angels concerning you... on their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.' Verbatim citation with formula 'it is written' — Scripture cited by the tempter, demonstrating the contest is over interpretation, not knowledge.

echoes.text: He was there with Yahweh forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread, nor drank water. He wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten commandments.
echoes.note: The forty days and forty nights of fasting (v.2) echoes Moses' forty days and nights on Sinai without bread or water (Exod 34:28; also Exod 24:18). Strong verbal and numeric match; the new-Moses typology recurs throughout Matthew (mountain, law-giver).

echoes.text: Your children shall be wanderers in the wilderness forty years, and shall bear your prostitution, until your dead bodies are consumed in the wilderness. After the number of the days in which you spied out the land, even forty days, for every day a year, you will bear your iniquities, even forty years, and you will know my alienation.’
echoes.note: Israel's forty years of wilderness wandering/testing (a year for each day of spying) stands behind Jesus' forty days. Hays' Thematic Coherence: each of Jesus' three answers is drawn from Deut's reflection on those forty years (manna, Massah, idolatry), framing Jesus as faithful Israel reduced to one obedient Son.

echoes.text: When I had gone up onto the mountain to receive the stone tablets, even the tablets of the covenant which Yahweh made with you, then I stayed on the mountain forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water.
echoes.note: Moses 'neither ate bread nor drank water forty days and forty nights' (Deut 9:9, 18) parallels Jesus' fast; Matthew's Deuteronomic quotation chain makes this Deuteronomy theophany-fast a likely background to the forty-day frame.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not.
echoes.note: The manna 'test' ('that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law') underlies the bread temptation; Deut 8:3 (quoted) is the interpretive lens, but Exod 16's hunger-and-bread test is the recurrent narrative source.

echoes.text: All the congregation of the children of Israel traveled from the wilderness of Sin, by their journeys, according to Yahweh’s commandment, and encamped in Rephidim; but there was no water for the people to drink. Therefore the people quarreled with Moses, and said, “Give us water to drink.” Moses said to them, “Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test Yahweh?” The people were thirsty for water there; and the people murmured against Moses, and said, “Why […]
echoes.note: Massah/Meribah, where Israel 'tested the LORD' demanding water — the very event Deut 6:16 names — supplies the recurrent background for the temple-pinnacle scene where Jesus refuses to put God to the test.

echoes.text: You shall remember all the way which Yahweh your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, to prove you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments, or not.
echoes.note: 'The LORD led you these forty years in the wilderness... testing you to know what was in your heart.' Verbal kinship with v.1 ('led up... into the wilderness to be tempted') and the whole framing of a divinely-led wilderness test.

echoes.text: You shall consider in your heart that as a man disciplines his son, so Yahweh your God disciplines you.
echoes.note: 'As a man disciplines his son, so the LORD your God disciplines you' — the father/son wilderness-discipline theme resonates with the repeated 'If you are the Son of God' challenge framing Jesus' wilderness testing.

echoes.text: You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus says Yahweh, Israel is my son, my firstborn, and I have said to you, “Let my son go, that he may serve me”; and you have refused to let him go. Behold, I will kill your son, your firstborn.’”
echoes.note: 'Israel is my firstborn son' — the divine-sonship of Israel that Jesus recapitulates; Satan's taunt 'If you are the Son of God' presses on the sonship just declared at the baptism (3:17) and rooted in Israel's corporate sonship.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely […]
echoes.note: The tempter ('serpent'/devil) offers food and god-like status; Eve's threefold desire (good for food, delight to eyes, to make wise) loosely patterns the three temptations (bread, spectacle, kingdoms). Adam typology: where the first man fell, Jesus stands. Disputed in detail, hence contested.

echoes.text: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” Then Satan […]
echoes.note: 'The Satan' (the adversary) granted access to test a righteous man under divine permission parallels the devil's testing role; the title 'Satan' Jesus uses (v.10) draws on this adversary figure.

echoes.text: Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, that is over against Jericho. Yahweh showed him all the land of Gilead, to Dan, and all Naphtali, and the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, and all the land of Judah, to the western sea, and the south, and the Plain of the valley of Jericho the city of palm trees, to Zoar. Yahweh said to him, “This is the land which I swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, saying, ‘I will give it to […]
echoes.note: From a high mountain Moses is shown all the land/kingdoms; the devil takes Jesus to 'an exceedingly high mountain' and shows him all the kingdoms of the world (v.8). The Moses-on-Pisgah panorama is inverted — a counterfeit Nebo offering the world by idolatry rather than promise.

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father. Ask of me, and I will give the nations for your inheritance, the uttermost parts of the earth for your possession.
echoes.note: The Father gives the Son 'the nations as your heritage'; Satan counterfeits this by offering 'all the kingdoms of the world' (v.8-9) on his own terms. Royal-Son enthronement (cf. 3:17 'my Son') makes the kingdoms-offer a parody of Ps 2's promised dominion.

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one. You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: The Shema's command to love/serve God with whole heart frames the cluster of Deut 6 citations; exclusive devotion to the one LORD is the theological center of Jesus' resistance.

echoes.text: Elijah came near to all the people, and said, “How long will you waver between the two sides? If Yahweh is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him.” The people answered him not a word.
echoes.note: The demand for undivided allegiance ('serve him only', v.10) recalls the Deuteronomic monotheism dramatized at Carmel; faint thematic recurrence of 'serve the LORD alone.'

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: Universal dominion over 'all peoples, nations' given to the Son of Man — the legitimate eschatological kingship the devil offers as a shortcut without the cross. Faint, thematic.

echoes.text: He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, “Arise and eat!” He looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on the coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and lay down again. Yahweh’s angel came again the second time, and touched him, and said, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.” He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty […]
echoes.note: Elijah in the wilderness, fed by an angel, journeys forty days; angels minister to Jesus after his forty-day wilderness fast (v.11). Recurrent prophet-in-wilderness, angelically-sustained pattern.

echoes.text: You will tread on the lion and cobra. You will trample the young lion and the serpent underfoot.
echoes.note: The verse immediately after Satan's quotation ('you will tread on the lion and the adder') promises mastery over the adversary — an ironic uncited remainder of Ps 91 that the narrative enacts as Jesus masters the devil.

echoes.text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”
echoes.note: 'The LORD rebuke you, Satan!' — the heavenly rebuke of the accuser resonates with Jesus' 'Get behind me, Satan!' (v.10). Faint verbal/thematic recurrence of rebuking the adversary.

harmony.title: The Temptation in the wilderness
harmony.note: Mark gives it in two verses; Matthew and Luke give the three temptations in full, though in differing order.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Into the wilderness the Spirit leads us, hungry and tried.
We do not live by bread alone.
Every word from the mouth of God is our bread.
We will worship the Lord and serve only him.
When we were caught and ashamed, God did not leave us.
You are our hiding place; you surround us with deliverance.
Come, let us worship the One who meets us in the wild.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Forty days the wilderness stretches before us: dry wind, bare stone, an empty stomach, a tempter's easy voice.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
You know this country. Adam knew it, reaching for the fruit; you walked it yourself, hungry and unbroken.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
So when the voice says turn these stones to bread, says bow down, says throw yourself down, teach us your one answer.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
For you are our hiding place; when we confess, the guilt we carried lifts like fog burning off.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
Come into the wilderness unafraid; the angels are already on their way. Come, let us worship.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Lead us through. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The Spirit drives us out where the bread runs out.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
We do not live by bread alone, but by God's every word.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
You are our hiding place; you surround us with deliverance.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
Come, let us worship the One who meets us in the wild.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.
